title: Let the children come (Mark 10:1–16)
hook: the disciples shoo the children, and he is indignant

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child in the middle, while the disciples argued about who was greatest. Your line was last of all. Where did you go last? Today, more children, and the disciples still haven't learned. Day two hundred eighteen.

Picture an important person visiting a town, and the security detail keeping the crowds back. Now picture the kids trying to get through. Jesus has crossed into Judea, on the far side of the Jordan, heading south toward Jerusalem. Crowds again. Teachers come with a hard question about marriage. And in the middle of all this serious business, parents start bringing their children to him, so he'll touch them. The disciples step in and scold the parents. He's busy. Not now. And for the only time in Mark, we're told Jesus was indignant.
screen: `KEEPING THE KIDS BACK.` → `ON THE ROAD TO JERUSALEM.` → `THE DISCIPLES SCOLD THE PARENTS.`

segments.voice: First, the question before it. Pharisees ask whether a man may divorce his wife. Jesus goes back past the Law to the beginning, to Genesis: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh. What God has joined, no one should separate. Catholics hear in these verses the root of the Church's teaching that a sacramental marriage is for life. Other Christians read the passage in other ways, and it's a tender subject in many families. Mark gives it in a few lines and moves on. Second, the scolding. The disciples rebuke the people bringing children. Maybe they're protecting him. Maybe kids just weren't important enough. Either way, they've forgotten yesterday already. Third, his anger. Mark's word is strong: indignant, much displeased. It's the only time Mark says it of Jesus. And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not; for of such is the kingdom of God." Suffer here is old English for allow. Let them come. Then he goes further: whoever doesn't receive the kingdom of God like a little child won't enter it. Not like a grown-up earning it. Like a child being handed it. Fourth, what he does. "And embracing them, and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them." Arms around them, hands on their heads, a blessing. This line is one reason the Church has long welcomed children, and one of the passages Catholics point to when they baptize infants, who can't earn anything, and simply receive.
screen: `FIRST, A QUESTION ABOUT MARRIAGE.` · `THE DISCIPLES SCOLD THE PARENTS.` · `INDIGNANT: LET THEM COME.` · `EMBRACED, TOUCHED, BLESSED.` · then, large: `OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive something like a child. Settle and breathe. A child doesn't earn a hug or a meal. They just open their hands. So open yours, palms up, on your lap. Now think of something good you've been handed lately and never quite received. A compliment you brushed off. Help you felt you had to pay back. Love you didn't think you'd earned. Let it land. Say thank you, out loud or inside. If you pray, you can receive it as a gift from God. The bell holds the time.
Let the children come. What Jesus says, indignant, when his disciples try to shoo the children away. Then he embraces and blesses them. Today's word.
Your line: of such is the kingdom. Today, the next time someone offers you something, don't argue or explain. Just say thank you and take it. Day two hundred eighteen.

screen: `DAY 218 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LOOKING ON HIM, LOVED HIM.`

howItsDone: The Catholic Church baptizes infants, and parishes often bless children at Mass who are too young to receive Communion; Mark 10:13–16 is among the passages read at infant baptisms.

fork.setup: you're a disciple. Jesus is in the middle of serious teaching, and parents keep pushing their kids forward. what do you do?
options: tell the parents to take the children away.
line the children up to meet him.
fork.reveal: the disciples scold the parents, and Jesus is indignant: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not."

original.note: Greek: he was indignant. Mark uses it of Jesus only here.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle picture of Jesus with kids.
what it means: he's angry that children were pushed away, and says the kingdom belongs to those who receive like them.
what a scholar hears: ēganaktēsen, strong indignation; the passage Catholics cite among the grounds for infant baptism.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 10:14 and 10:16 given from memory; confirm.

Marriage and divorce (10:1–12) handled in a few lines: the Catholic teaching on indissolubility of sacramental marriage is stated, other Christians' readings acknowledged without detail. This is pastorally sensitive; a Keeper should review tone.
'The only time Mark says Jesus was indignant' (aganakteō of Jesus only at 10:14 in Mark): confirm.
Mark 10:13–16 as a reading option in the Rite of Baptism for Children, and its use in arguments for infant baptism (cf. CCC 1244, 1250): confirm catechism references.
Blessing of young children at Communion is a common parish custom, not a universal rubric; phrased 'often'.
